Comment on Proposed Rule RIN 2900-AS31

I am a veteran who has benefited from VA healthcare and who believes strongly in protecting taxpayer resources. I do not support taxpayer funding for elective abortion services that reverse prior personal decisions. However, I oppose the proposed rule’s removal of coverage for cases of rape, incest, and medically necessary pregnancy care.

This rule, if finalized, would harm survivors of military sexual trauma, as well as veterans facing life-threatening or non-viable pregnancies. These circumstances are not “elective”—they are medical crises. Denying such care results in higher costs for the system (due to emergency complications), poorer health outcomes, and unnecessary suffering.

The evidence is clear: abortion denial has been linked to increased maternal morbidity, higher infant mortality, worsened mental health, greater economic hardship, and prolonged exposure to violent partners. Veterans are at unique risk, with nearly four in ten women reporting sexual assault or harassment during service.

I urge the VA to revise the rule to preserve exceptions for rape, incest, life- or health-endangering pregnancies, and miscarriage/ectopic care. This balance respects taxpayer concerns while fulfilling VA’s duty under 38 U.S.C. §1710 to promote the health and well-being of enrolled veterans.

For full supporting evidence, please see the attached PDF appendix.

Respectfully submitted,
Michael K. Harris Sr.

===== FILE 18670__1.pdf =====
Supporting Evidence ‒ RIN 2900-AS31 Public Comment
This appendix provides supporting evidence on the health, mental health, and economic outcomes
associated with denial of abortion and miscarriage-related healthcare. Each citation is drawn from
peer-reviewed studies, government reports, or established research institutes. These references are
submitted to support my comment opposing the removal of coverage for rape, incest, and medically
necessary care under the Department of Veterans Affairs proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31.
Maternal and Infant Health Harms
• A 2025 JAMA analysis found higher-than-expected infant mortality rates in states with abortion bans,
including ̃478 excess infant deaths (JAMA 2025).
• Studies show pregnancy-associated mortality increased ̃8% in ban states after Dobbs (University of
Colorado/University of Maryland analysis, 2024).
• Documented cases show women with previable rupture of membranes or septic miscarriage faced
delayed care, resulting in higher risk of sepsis and hemorrhage (KFF 2023; JAMA Network Open
2023).
Mental Health Impacts
• The Turnaway Study (ANSIRH, UCSF) found women denied abortions experienced more anxiety,
stress, and lower self-esteem than those who received care.
• Over five years, women denied care had worse physical and economic outcomes than women who
obtained abortions (ANSIRH 2018).
Violence and Safety
• Research shows women denied abortions were more likely to remain in contact with violent partners,
while those receiving care were more likely to escape abusive relationships (Foster et al., Lancet Public
Health 2018).
Economic Consequences
• The Turnaway Study and follow-up analyses show that being denied an abortion increases poverty,
debt, and likelihood of eviction.
• A 2022 NBER working paper confirmed denial of abortion correlates with long-term financial
instability for families.
System-Level Harms to Healthcare Delivery
• Abortion bans erode OB-GYN training, reduce availability of emergency miscarriage and ectopic
care, and create occupational health risks for providers (ACOG, JAMA Network Open 2023).

Military Sexual Trauma Context
• Meta-analysis shows ̃38% of women veterans report MST (sexual harassment or assault during
service). Denying abortion access in MST-related pregnancies conflicts with VA’s mandate under 38
U.S.C. §1710.
• VA resources acknowledge MST prevalence and prioritize trauma-informed care for survivors;
coverage carve-outs are essential.
